verse.text: For the vision is yet for an appointed time, but at the end it shall speak, and not lie: though it tarry, wait for it; because it will surely come, it will not tarry.
verse.summary: Habakkuk had cried out to God about violence and delay, then climbed his watchtower to see what God would answer. The answer was to write the vision down plainly — and to understand that God's promises run on an appointed time, not an anxious one. "Though it tarry, wait for it" doesn't contradict "it will not tarry": what feels late to you is never late to Him. If something God spoke over your life seems overdue today, keep it written, keep watching, and keep waiting — it will surely come.

sermon.title: Go Again Seven Times
sermon.excerpt: Six times the servant looked toward the sea and came back with the same report: there is nothing. Elijah never argued with the report — he just said, go again. The seventh time, a cloud like a man's hand, and the prophet told the king to get his chariot ready.

bibleStudy.title: Lazarus, Come Forth

verses.text: Then said Martha unto Jesus, Lord, if thou hadst been here, my brother had not died. But I know, that even now, whatsoever thou wilt ask of God, he will give it thee. Jesus saith unto her, Thy brother shall rise again. Martha saith unto him, I know that he shall rise again in the resurrection at the last day. Jesus said unto her, I am the resurrection, and the life: he that believeth in me, though he were dead, yet shall he live: And whosoever liveth and believeth in me shall never die. Believest thou this? She saith unto him, Yea, Lord: I believe that thou art the Christ, the Son of God, which should come into the world.

When Jesus therefore saw her weeping, and the Jews also weeping which came with her, he groaned in the spirit, and was troubled, And said, Where have ye laid him? They said unto him, Lord, come and see. Jesus wept. Then said the Jews, Behold how he loved him! ... Then they took away the stone from the place where the dead was laid. And Jesus lifted up his eyes, and said, Father, I thank thee that thou hast heard me. And I knew that thou hearest me always: but because of the people which stand by I said it, that they may believe that thou hast sent me. And when he had thus spoken, he cried with a loud voice, Lazarus, come forth. And he that was dead came forth, bound hand and foot with graveclothes: and his face was bound with a napkin. Jesus said unto them, Loose him, and let him go.
But if the Spirit of him that raised up Christ from the dead dwell in you, he that raised up Christ from the dead shall also quicken your mortal bodies by his Spirit that dwelleth in you.

bibleStudy.excerpt: Martha told Jesus flat out that He was too late by her own count, four days too late — and He answered the accusation not with an explanation but by walking to the grave and calling a dead man by his own name.
body: Start with the sentence John refuses to let you skip past: "Now Jesus loved Martha, and her sister, and Lazarus." Underline loved. Then read the very next thing that love does, and let it unsettle you a little, because it's supposed to. Word comes that the one He loves is sick. Jesus does not drop what He's doing. He does not run. He stays exactly where He is for two more days, on purpose, while a family He genuinely loved buried a man He could have healed with a sentence from a distance, the same way He'd already healed a centurion's servant and a nobleman's son without ever setting foot in the house. This is not a story about a Savior who didn't get there in time. This is a story about a Savior who was never trying to get there in time, because He had already decided time wasn't going to be the main character in this one.

So Martha meets Him on the road outside the village, and the first thing out of her mouth is not worship — it's an indictment, dressed up in respectful language but an indictment all the same: "Lord, if thou hadst been here, my brother had not died." That's grief talking, and grief is allowed to talk like that. But watch what she does in the very next breath, without being asked to walk it back: "But I know, that even now, whatsoever thou wilt ask of God, he will give it thee." She doesn't retract the accusation. She just refuses to let it be the last word. You can tell God exactly where you think He was late and still, in the same sentence, keep believing He isn't finished. Those two things are not opposites. Martha just taught you how to hold both at once.

Jesus doesn't argue the timeline with her either. He goes straight for doctrine, and not future-tense doctrine — present-tense doctrine, aimed directly at the moment she's standing in: "I am the resurrection, and the life." Not "I will perform a resurrection." Not "I know a guy who can." I am. Present tense, first person, the same formula God used at the burning bush, now wearing sandals on a dirt road outside a graveyard. Martha was thinking funeral theology — someday, at the last day, in the sweet by and by. Jesus corrects the tense of her faith before He ever corrects the location of her brother. Then He asks her the one question this whole study is actually built around: "Believest thou this?" Not "do you believe resurrection is a doctrine." Do you believe it's standing in front of you right now.

Mary comes out next, and she uses Martha's exact same four accusing words — word for word, "Lord, if thou hadst been here, my brother had not died" — which tells you this sentence had been rehearsed in that house for four straight days. Grief repeats itself. But Mary delivers hers from the floor, falling at His feet, where Martha delivered hers standing upright and ready to argue theology. Same complaint, two completely different postures, and Jesus does not correct either woman for how she brought it. What He does instead is the verse that should wreck every bad theology you've ever absorbed about tears being the opposite of faith: He sees her weeping, the crowd weeping, and — knowing full well He's about to raise the man in four minutes — He groans in His spirit, gets troubled, and weeps Himself. Let that land. The Man who already knows the ending still lets Himself feel the middle. If you've ever been told that crying means you don't really believe, Jesus just modeled the alternative two verses before He performed the actual miracle.

Then comes my favorite unflattering detail in the whole Gospel, the one nobody puts on a greeting card. Jesus says, "Take away the stone," and Martha — practical to the very last, grief and logistics running on the same track — says, essentially, don't do that, he's been in there four days, by this time he stinketh. I love her for that line, because it means nobody sanitized this story for you. Martha believed enough to argue theology on the road and still believed the body would smell. Jesus doesn't rebuke her nose. He rebukes her sequence: "Said I not unto thee, that, if thou wouldest believe, thou shouldest see the glory of God?" Not see it and then believe. Believe it, and then see it. Faith was never supposed to wait for the smell to go away on its own. Faith is what you keep walking in while the smell is still very much present.

And look at what He does before He ever raises His voice toward the tomb — He prays, out loud, in front of everyone, and He tells you exactly why: "Father, I thank thee that thou hast heard me. And I knew that thou hearest me always: but because of the people which stand by I said it, that they may believe that thou hast sent me." The prayer wasn't for information. He already had the answer before He asked. He prayed it out loud for the crowd's sake, not His own — which means even Jesus, in His own earthly ministry, modeled praying publicly not to manufacture an answer, but to let other people watch the relationship that already produces one. Some of your prayers are for you. Some of them are for the people standing close enough to watch what happens when you pray them.

Then the sentence this whole study is named for: "He cried with a loud voice, Lazarus, come forth." Notice He didn't shout "dead man, arise," or "whoever's in there, come out." He called a name. A specific, personal, already-decomposing name. Here's my real question for you today — what in your life have you stopped calling by name, because it's been dead long enough that you quietly reclassified it as gone instead of sleeping? Your marriage. Your ministry. Your health report. Your finances. Your joy. Grief eventually talks itself into speaking about the dead thing in general terms — "it's over," "that door's closed" — because naming it again means hoping again, and hoping again means risking the grief all over. Jesus skipped that entire caution. He walked up to a sealed, stinking tomb and used the dead man's actual name, like a man expecting an answer. And Paul tells you, writing to ordinary believers centuries later, that the very same Spirit who did that is not a historical artifact — "if the Spirit of him that raised up Christ from the dead dwell in you, he that raised up Christ from the dead shall also quicken your mortal bodies by his Spirit that dwelleth in you." That voice didn't retire after Bethany. It's living in you right now, on lease, waiting on you to point it at something you've gone quiet about.

And he that was dead came forth — bound hand and foot with graveclothes, his face still wrapped in a napkin, walking blind and mummified out of a tomb because a word was stronger than a four-day decomposition. But notice the miracle doesn't end with Lazarus upright. Jesus' very next sentence is a job assignment for the people standing around: "Loose him, and let him go." The resurrection was His to speak. The unwrapping was theirs to do. That is the whole doctrine of the church in one clause — God does what only God can do, and then He turns to the people standing closest to the miracle and says, now you go deal with the graveclothes. Somebody in your life got raised and is still walking around half-wrapped in the evidence of where they used to be, waiting on somebody who actually loves them to start pulling at the linen instead of just marveling from a safe distance at the fact that they're breathing again.

So carry all three pieces out of Bethany. Carry Martha's honesty, which argued with God on the road and believed Him anyway in the very same breath. Carry Mary's weeping, which Jesus never once treated as evidence of weak faith. And carry the stone, rolled away not because the body had somehow gotten less dead, but because somebody finally obeyed the instruction before the miracle instead of after it. Whatever you've been quietly calling finished, stop calling it that. Go stand at the mouth of it, say its name out loud like you expect an answer, and start rolling away whatever stone you've been using as an excuse not to find out. He is still the resurrection. He is still the life. And He is still calling dead things by name. In Jesus' name, amen.

lines: Father, I declare today that I will not stop praying because the horizon says nothing — Your word over my life is already settled in heaven!
I hear the sound of abundance of rain before I ever see a cloud!
I bow low, I press in, and I pray until the answer comes down!
Six nothings will not talk me out of my seventh time — I go again!
I will not faint and I will not be weary in well doing — in due season I shall reap!
The vision is for an appointed time; though it tarry, I wait for it, because it will surely come!
I will not despise the day of small things — that cloud like a man's hand is the hand of my God rising for me!
After the drought comes abundance — over my health, my home, my finances and my children!
I prepare my chariot today, because the rain is on its way and nothing will stop it!
Save this. Speak it over your house today. I go again, and the rain is coming! In Jesus' mighty name, amen!

dreamFire.title: Chariots of Fire Surround Me
dreamFire.intro: Tonight's shield prayer is not a guess at your dream — it is Elisha's open-eyed vision loosed ahead of you into the dark: a mountain full of horses and chariots of fire stationed round about you before any enemy arrives. Pray it out loud and let the fire take its position before you sleep.
points: Father, as You opened the eyes of Elisha's servant, open the eyes of my spirit tonight and let me see what is already true — horses and chariots of fire stationed round about me, before my bed, behind my back, and over every border of my sleep, in the mighty name of Jesus!

Every evil altar lit anywhere on my account tonight, every candle struck, every incantation spoken over my name — a chariot of fire rides in before the rite is finished, and that altar goes up in flames, in the name of Jesus!

Every power that rises to chase me, waits to trap me, or schemes to trade my portion for another's in the dream realm tonight runs straight into a wall of horsemen it never saw coming and is scattered, in Jesus' mighty name!

Every mark, ring, garment, or covering any hand dares lift toward me while I sleep tonight catches fire in the hand that holds it and falls to ash before it ever reaches my skin, in the name of Jesus!

Every witchcraft table, coven, or secret session convened tonight to study my file, call my name, or cast a vote over my life looks up to find chariots of fire ringing the room and scatters in terror, in Jesus' mighty name!
Every pit dug, net spread, or snare set along my path between midnight and daybreak — the wheels of fire roll over it first, and the digger falls into what was dug for me, in the name of Jesus!

Every gate assigned to work against me tonight — gate of delay, gate of sickness, gate of confusion, gate of sudden loss — finds a chariot of fire parked across its threshold and shall not open, in the mighty name of Jesus!

If my spirit has been summoned, detained, or carried anywhere outside my ring of fire tonight, I sound the trumpet of recall now — mount up on chariots of fire and bring me home, spirit, soul, and body, whole and untouched, in Jesus' mighty name!

Let the same mountain full of horses and chariots ring my household tonight — every room, every bed, every name under this roof — so that no darkness assigned against this house finds a way past the fire, in the name of Jesus!

Every evil court, secret tribunal, or night session convened to pass a verdict on my life while I rest meets a chariot of fire standing at its gate — your judgment is turned back, and I appeal to a better Court whose Judge is my Father, in Jesus' mighty name!

So I decree over tonight: the mountain is full of horses, the valley is full of fire, and I am not the one surrounded — my enemies are. I will rise in the morning exactly as I lay down: covered, untouched, and victorious, in the mighty, all-consuming name of Jesus Christ, amen! 🔥
